title: The meat question
hookLine: Sikhs hold different views on eating meat; the code forbids ritually slaughtered meat only

lines: DAL ON ONE PLATE, CHICKEN ON ONE.
cards: A family birthday, buffet style. Two cousins in line, both with a steel kara on the wrist, both wearing a turban. One fills a plate with dal, rice and paneer.
The other adds a piece of tandoori chicken. Neither comments. An aunt watching from the end of the table has opinions, and keeps them for later.
Ask Sikhs whether a Sikh can eat meat and the answers differ, sometimes inside one household. Today is that question, and what the Sikh code actually says.

teach.h: THE CODE: NO RITUALLY KILLED MEAT.
teach.b: Start with the code; this path met its four things avoided back on day two hundred seventy. The Sikh Rehat Maryada lists a few things an initiated Sikh must never do.
One is eating kutha, meat from an animal killed by ritual slaughter. Its readers notice what the line doesn't say: it doesn't forbid all meat.

teach.h: JHATKA FOR SOME, NO MEAT FOR OTHERS.
teach.b: So some Sikhs eat meat killed with a single quick stroke, called jhatka, and see no conflict. Others read the whole spirit of Gurbani as pointing away from killing for food, and keep a vegetarian life.

Some streams met earlier in this block, like the Namdharis, keep a vegetarian kitchen as a community. And the langar, the free kitchen, is traditionally vegetarian, so anyone of any diet can sit and eat the same meal.
Now the Granth. In a passage on Ang 1289, Guru Nanak turns to people quarreling over flesh.
In paraphrase: fools argue about meat, yet know nothing of spiritual wisdom or meditation. Readers hear that line in different ways. Some hear the Guru saying the argument itself misses the point.
Others notice the passage goes on to observe that people are born of flesh, and read it as cutting through purity rules.
Near the end of the Granth, couplets of Kabir speak sharply against killing, and some vegetarian Sikhs turn to them.

teach.h: BOTH SIDES OPEN THE SAME BOOK.
teach.b: So both sides open the same book.

teach.h: A LANGAR WHERE EVERY PLATE MATCHES.
teach.b: What they share is the line the code draws: no ritual slaughter, and a langar where every plate can be the same.

how: Sikhs follow different diets: the Rehat Maryada forbids initiated Sikhs to eat kutha, ritually slaughtered meat; some Sikhs eat jhatka meat, others are vegetarian, and the langar is traditionally vegetarian so that all can share it.

o: a fast from meat during one holy month
how Sikhs differ on whether to eat meat
a rule that meat may be served in langar

games.q: inside the meat question: tap the pairs.
p: meat killed with a single quick stroke

s: the Sikh code forbids all meat
its line is against kutha, ritually slaughtered meat. Sikhs differ on the rest.
so anyone, of any diet, can eat the same meal.
only one side of the debate quotes the Granth
both sides open the same book: Guru Nanak on Ang 1289, and Kabir's couplets near the end.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, and people are quarreling over whether meat is pure. what do you say?
o: fools argue about flesh, and know nothing of wisdom or meditation.
eat whatever you like; nothing matters.
games.why: on Ang 1289 he turns the argument back on the arguers. readers still differ on what that means for the plate.

practice: Think of one person whose plate looks different from yours, a vegetarian friend, a cousin who fasts, a coworker who keeps a rule you don't, and picture sitting across from them at one table.
Let any small urge to comment go out with the breath, and think of one dish you could both share; if you pray, hold that table before Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: The meat question. Sikhs differ on eating meat; the code draws its line at ritually slaughtered meat, and the langar keeps one vegetarian table for all. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: different plates. The same book on both sides, and one langar for all. Until tomorrow.
